dok_rationale: Part (c) requires bounding a conclusion: the student must separate a descriptive claim about the 12 students measured from a causal, generalizing claim about the whole school, cite the feature of the data or its collection that settles each, and name the missing evidence; both claims sound alike and either can be partly defended, so the reasoning is what is scored.
stem: Suppose the school newspaper surveyed the 12 students in one AP Statistics class on a quiz day. The table shows each student's hours of sleep the night before and their score on that day's 10-point quiz. The editors are choosing between two headlines.\par\smallskip 	extbf{Claim 1:} ``In this class, students who slept more tended to score higher.''\par 	extbf{Claim 2:} ``Sleeping more raises quiz scores for all students at our school.''
first_take: Which claim would you print in the newspaper? One sentence. No wrong answers yet.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Who are the individuals in this data set? Name the two variables, and state whether each one is categorical or quantitative.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: In one or two sentences, describe what the table shows about sleep and quiz scores \emph{for this class}, in context. Name the student who does not fit the pattern.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Decide which claim these data can support and which they cannot. For each claim, cite the specific feature of the data --- or of how the data were collected --- that settles it. Then name 	extbf{one} kind of data the newspaper would need to collect before it could print Claim 2.

answers.a: Individuals: the 12 students in the class (one per row). Variables: hours of sleep last night (quantitative, hours) and score on today's quiz (quantitative, points out of 10). The name column labels the row; it is not a variable under study.
answers.b: In this class, students who slept more generally scored higher: the 5--6 hour sleepers scored 4--6 points while the 8--9 hour sleepers scored 8--10. Leo is the exception --- 4.5 hours of sleep but a score of 9 --- so the pattern is a tendency, not a rule. Context (this class, this quiz, hours and points) must be present.
answers.c: Claim 1 is supported. It only describes these 12 students (``in this class'', ``tended to''), and the table shows that tendency directly: scores rise with sleep across the rows, with Leo as the single exception, which ``tended to'' already allows. Claim 2 is not supported. Either feature settles it: (1) scope --- the data describe 12 students in one class on one day, not ``all students at our school'', so the claim reaches beyond the individuals measured; (2) cause --- the students chose their own sleep, nobody assigned it, so other differences between the students (study time, interest, when they did homework) could explain the pattern; ``raises'' is a cause-and-effect word this table cannot back. One kind of missing data (any one earns credit): a random sample of students from the whole school; an experiment in which students are randomly assigned different amounts of sleep; measurements of other variables such as study time; the same students on many quiz days.

expectedElements.description: Says Claim 1 is supported and ties it to the tendency visible in the table for this class (a description, not a cause)
Cites a settling feature: 12 students in one class are not all students at the school (scope), and/or sleep was chosen not assigned so other explanations remain (cause)
Names one specific kind of data: a random sample of the school, random assignment of sleep, another variable measured, or repeated quiz days

scoringGuide.E: Claim 1 supported with the tendency named, Claim 2 rejected with a scope or cause feature stated in context, and one specific kind of missing data named.
scoringGuide.P: Correct decisions on both claims but the settling feature is vague (``not enough data'', ``only 12 people'') with no link to scope or cause, OR a specific feature but no missing data named, OR Leo is used to reject Claim 1.
scoringGuide.I: Prints Claim 2 as supported, or rejects both claims, or gives no feature of the data or of how they were collected.

commonMistakes: Rejects Claim 1 because of Leo --- one exception does not erase a tendency, and ``tended to'' already allows it
Says ``12 is too small'' as the only reason --- size is not the issue; who was measured and how is
Treats ``slept more, scored higher'' and ``sleeping more raises scores'' as the same sentence
Names ``more students'' as the missing data without saying which students (a random sample of the school) or how (random assignment of sleep)

sentence_frames: Claim  lank[0.4in] is supported because, for these  lank[0.9in], the table shows  lank[2.2in].
Claim  lank[0.4in] is not supported because the data only describe  lank[1.6in] and the students  lank[1.5in] their own sleep.

dok_rationale: Placing a bare number into context and stating one thing it cannot tell a reader applies the lesson's idea in one known step, with no judgment between competing claims.
stem: A friend looks at the sleep-and-quiz table and says: ``The average score is 7.5, so this class knows the material.'' Write one sentence that gives the number 7.5 its context (what was measured, on whom, out of how many points), and one sentence naming something the number 7.5 by itself \emph{cannot} tell a reader.

answers.a: Context: 7.5 is the mean score, out of 10 points, on one quiz, for the 12 students in this one class on one day. Cannot tell: how spread out the scores were (they run from 4 to 10), whether other classes did as well, whether this quiz was easy, or how the class will do on the next quiz. Any one limit with the context sentence earns credit.
